name: Set
quick: A collection determined entirely by which objects belong to it.
definition: An object either is or is not a member of a set. Order and repeated listings do not change membership. Two sets are equal exactly when they have the same elements.
confusion: A set containing a number is not that number; braces matter.

name: Element
quick: An object belonging to a set.
definition: The statement $x\in A$ means that $x$ is an element of $A$. An element can itself be a set, but membership and containment as a subset remain different questions.
example: For $A=\{1,\{2\}\}$, the set $\{2\}$ is an element of $A$, while the number 2 is not.
confusion: Do not remove a layer of braces when deciding what objects are listed.

name: Singleton
quick: A set with exactly one element.
definition: A singleton has cardinality one, regardless of what its sole element is.
confusion: The empty set has no elements, whereas the set containing the empty set has one.

name: Set-builder notation
quick: A description of a set by a domain and a membership condition.
definition: In $\{x\in D:P(x)\}$, braces collect exactly the elements of $D$ satisfying $P$. The colon is read “such that”; some authors use a vertical separator instead.
confusion: The domain matters. A real-valued condition and the same integer-valued condition may select different elements.

name: Finite cardinality
quick: The number of distinct elements of a finite set.
definition: For a finite set $A$, the notation $|A|$ counts each distinct element once. Repeated appearances in a written list add no new elements. Infinite-set cardinality is a broader concept; the subtraction formulas here concern finite sets.
confusion: These bars count members of a set; bars around a number ordinarily mean absolute value.

name: Subset
quick: A set whose every element also belongs to another set.
definition: $A\subseteq B$ means that for every object $x$, $x\in A$ implies $x\in B$. Equality is permitted, and the empty set is a subset of every set.
example: $\{1\}\subseteq\{1,2\}$ because its only element belongs to the second set.
confusion: Subset compares sets by their members; $\{1\}\in\{1,2\}$ is false even though the subset claim is true.

name: Proper subset
quick: A subset that is not equal to the containing set.
definition: $A\subsetneq B$ requires both $A\subseteq B$ and $A\ne B$. Thus $B$ has at least one element missing from $A$.
confusion: The notation $\subset$ is ambiguous across authors; this course uses $\subsetneq$ for strict containment.

name: Union
quick: The set of elements belonging to at least one of the given sets.
definition: $A\cup B$ contains $x$ exactly when $x\in A$ or $x\in B$, using inclusive OR. Common members occur only once in the resulting set.
confusion: Union includes the overlap; it does not mean exactly one set.

name: Intersection
quick: The set of elements belonging to all of the given sets.
definition: $A\cap B$ contains precisely the objects that belong to both $A$ and $B$. For three sets, a member of their intersection must belong to all three.
confusion: Nonempty pairwise intersections do not guarantee a member common to three sets.

name: Set difference
quick: The elements of the first set that do not belong to the second.
definition: $A\setminus B$ contains $x$ exactly when $x\in A$ and $x\notin B$. Order matters.
confusion: This is an operation on membership, not subtraction of the set sizes.

name: Universe for sets
quick: A fixed surrounding set containing all elements under discussion.
definition: When using complements, every set under discussion is a subset of the chosen universe $U$. The universe determines which objects can lie outside a particular set.
confusion: A universe contains the members of the discussed sets; it need not contain those sets themselves as elements.

name: Complement
quick: The elements of the fixed universe that do not belong to a set.
definition: Relative to a universe $U$, the complement $A^c$ is $U\setminus A$. All complements in a single identity must use the same universe.
confusion: The superscript c is a complement marker, not a numerical exponent.

name: Disjoint sets
quick: Sets with no common element.
definition: Two sets are disjoint exactly when their intersection is empty. A collection is pairwise disjoint when every two different sets in it are disjoint.
example: $\{1,3\}$ and $\{2,4\}$ are disjoint. The empty set is disjoint from itself.
confusion: Different sets need not be disjoint: $\{1,2\}$ and $\{2,3\}$ differ but share 2.

name: Symmetric difference
quick: The elements belonging to exactly one of two sets.
definition: $A\mathbin{\triangle}B=(A\setminus B)\cup(B\setminus A)$. It includes both exclusive parts and excludes the common part.
confusion: The triangular symbol here names a set operation, not a geometric triangle.

name: Element proof
quick: A proof of a set claim by following an arbitrary element through membership definitions.
definition: To prove inclusion, start with any member of the first set and show it belongs to the second. For equality, prove both inclusions or give a chain of equivalent membership conditions.
example: If $x\in A\cap B$, then $x\in A$ by the definition of intersection; hence $A\cap B\subseteq A$.
confusion: A selected example cannot establish a universal inclusion, and one inclusion alone cannot establish equality.

name: De Morgan’s laws for sets
quick: Complementing a union gives the intersection of the complements; complementing an intersection gives their union.
definition: In a common universe, $(A\cup B)^c=A^c\cap B^c$ and $(A\cap B)^c=A^c\cup B^c$. These follow from the corresponding logical laws applied to membership.
example: An object outside the union is outside both sets, so it lies in both complements.
confusion: Use a common universe for every complement.

name: Venn diagram
quick: A region drawing used to display combinations of set membership.
definition: Closed regions represent sets inside a rectangle for the universe. An object in an overlap belongs to both sets. Shading can indicate the members selected by an operation.
example: For $A=\{1,2\}$ and $B=\{2,3\}$, place 2 in the overlap, 1 only in A, and 3 only in B.
confusion: Area does not represent cardinality, and a single drawing does not prove a general identity.

name: Power set
quick: The set of all subsets of a given set.
definition: The notation $\mathcal P(A)$ collects all sets $B$ such that $B\subseteq A$. If $A$ has $n$ elements, independent inclusion or exclusion of each gives $2^n$ subsets.
confusion: Members of the power set are subsets, not necessarily members of the original set.

name: Bit
quick: A digit with one of the two values 0 and 1.
definition: A bit can record one binary choice, such as whether a feature is excluded (0) or included (1). A sequence of bits can record several independent choices.
example: For two features a and b, the bits 10 include a and exclude b.
confusion: A bit is a digit, not the whole collection of feature choices.

name: Bit mask
quick: A collection of bits with one position assigned to each feature or membership choice.
definition: Once the feature order is fixed, each position says whether its feature belongs to the selected subset. For n features there are $2^n$ masks.
example: With features a,b in that order, 00, 10, 01, 11 encode the four subsets.
confusion: Bit positions have an order so they can name features; the subset itself does not have an order.

name: Ordered pair
quick: A record with a first and a second entry, whose positions matter.
definition: The pairs $(a,b)$ and $(c,d)$ are equal exactly when $a=c$ and $b=d$. Unlike sets, reversing their entries can change the object.
confusion: Parentheses for an ordered pair are not braces for a two-element set.

name: Cartesian product
quick: The set of all ordered pairs with first entry in one set and second entry in another.
definition: $A\times B=\{(a,b):a\in A\text{ and }b\in B\}$. For finite sets its size is $|A||B|$. If either factor is empty, there are no complete pairs.
confusion: The multiplication-shaped symbol acts on sets here; the output is a set of pairs, not a number.

name: Inclusion–exclusion
quick: Counting a finite union by correcting the repeated counting of overlaps.
definition: For two finite sets, $|A\cup B|=|A|+|B|-|A\cap B|$. For three sets, add individual sizes, subtract each pairwise intersection, and add the triple intersection.
example: If 24 people use Python, 18 use JavaScript, and 10 use both, then $24+18-10=32$ use at least one.
confusion: Pairwise intersections include members of the triple intersection; they do not mean exactly two sets.

name: Partition
quick: A collection of nonempty, pairwise disjoint blocks covering a set.
definition: Every element of the set must belong to exactly one block. Nonemptiness excludes empty blocks, disjointness excludes overlap, and coverage excludes missing elements.
confusion: The empty collection partitions the empty set; a collection containing an empty block does not.

name: Block of a partition
quick: One of the nonempty subsets making up a partition.
definition: Different blocks cannot share an element, and every element of the partitioned set occurs in a block.
example: In the even/odd partition of the integers, the even integers form one block and the odd integers another.
confusion: A block need not have the same size as another block.

name: Indexed family
quick: A collection in which an index label selects each member.
definition: A family $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ assigns a set $A_i$ to each index $i$ in an index set $I$. The union asks for membership in at least one indexed set; the intersection asks for membership in all.
example: For $I=\{1,2\}$, let $A_1=\{a,b\}$ and $A_2=\{b,c\}$. Their union is $\{a,b,c\}$ and intersection is $\{b\}$.
confusion: An index is a label, not necessarily a numerical value or an element of the set it labels.

name: Index
quick: A label selecting a member of an indexed family.
definition: In $A_i$, read “A sub i,” the subscript i selects a set. The allowed labels form the index set I. The same labeling idea will be used for sequence terms.
example: The labels 1 and 2 select $A_1$ and $A_2$ in a two-set family.
confusion: The label need not belong to the set it identifies.

name: ⊆ — is a subset of
quick: A set whose every element also belongs to another set.
definition: $A\subseteq B$ means that for every object $x$, $x\in A$ implies $x\in B$. Equality is permitted, and the empty set is a subset of every set.
example: $\{1\}\subseteq\{1,2\}$ because its only element belongs to the second set.
confusion: Subset compares sets by their members; $\{1\}\in\{1,2\}$ is false even though the subset claim is true.

name: ⊊ — is a proper subset of
quick: A subset that is not equal to the containing set.
definition: $A\subsetneq B$ requires both $A\subseteq B$ and $A\ne B$. Thus $B$ has at least one element missing from $A$.
confusion: The notation $\subset$ is ambiguous across authors; this course uses $\subsetneq$ for strict containment.

name: ∪ — union
quick: The set of elements belonging to at least one of the given sets.
definition: $A\cup B$ contains $x$ exactly when $x\in A$ or $x\in B$, using inclusive OR. Common members occur only once in the resulting set.
confusion: Union includes the overlap; it does not mean exactly one set.

name: ∩ — intersection
quick: The set of elements belonging to all of the given sets.
definition: $A\cap B$ contains precisely the objects that belong to both $A$ and $B$. For three sets, a member of their intersection must belong to all three.
confusion: Nonempty pairwise intersections do not guarantee a member common to three sets.

name: ∖ — set difference
quick: The elements of the first set that do not belong to the second.
definition: $A\setminus B$ contains $x$ exactly when $x\in A$ and $x\notin B$. Order matters.
confusion: This is an operation on membership, not subtraction of the set sizes.

name: Aᶜ — complement
quick: The elements of the fixed universe that do not belong to a set.
definition: Relative to a universe $U$, the complement $A^c$ is $U\setminus A$. All complements in a single identity must use the same universe.
confusion: The superscript c is a complement marker, not a numerical exponent.

name: |A| — finite cardinality
quick: The number of distinct elements of a finite set.
definition: For a finite set $A$, the notation $|A|$ counts each distinct element once. Repeated appearances in a written list add no new elements. Infinite-set cardinality is a broader concept; the subtraction formulas here concern finite sets.
confusion: These bars count members of a set; bars around a number ordinarily mean absolute value.

name: 𝒫(A) — power set
quick: The set of all subsets of a given set.
definition: The notation $\mathcal P(A)$ collects all sets $B$ such that $B\subseteq A$. If $A$ has $n$ elements, independent inclusion or exclusion of each gives $2^n$ subsets.
confusion: Members of the power set are subsets, not necessarily members of the original set.

name: × — Cartesian product
quick: The set of all ordered pairs with first entry in one set and second entry in another.
definition: $A\times B=\{(a,b):a\in A\text{ and }b\in B\}$. For finite sets its size is $|A||B|$. If either factor is empty, there are no complete pairs.
confusion: The multiplication-shaped symbol acts on sets here; the output is a set of pairs, not a number.

name: △ — symmetric difference
quick: The elements belonging to exactly one of two sets.
definition: $A\mathbin{\triangle}B=(A\setminus B)\cup(B\setminus A)$. It includes both exclusive parts and excludes the common part.
confusion: The triangular symbol here names a set operation, not a geometric triangle.

name: ⋃ — indexed union
quick: The elements belonging to at least one set in the indexed family.
definition: For sets $A_i$ labeled by indices $i$ in $I$, $\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i$ contains an object $x$ exactly when $x\in A_i$ for at least one index $i\in I$. Read this as “the union of A sub i over all i in I.” The union of a family with no indices is empty.
example: With $I=\{1,2\}$, $A_1=\{a,b\}$ and $A_2=\{b,c\}$, the indexed union is $\{a,b,c\}$.
confusion: One successful membership test is enough for union; intersection requires every test to succeed.

name: ⋂ — indexed intersection
quick: The elements belonging to every set in the indexed family.
definition: For subsets $A_i$ of a fixed universe $U$, $\bigcap_{i\in I}A_i$ contains an object $x\in U$ exactly when $x\in A_i$ for every index $i\in I$. Read this as “the intersection of A sub i over all i in I.” With no indices, every object in $U$ satisfies the condition, so the empty intersection is $U$.
example: With $I=\{1,2\}$, $A_1=\{a,b\}$ and $A_2=\{b,c\}$, the indexed intersection is $\{b\}$.
confusion: The empty-family convention needs a fixed universe. It is different from intersecting a nonempty family that includes the empty set, which gives the empty set.
